intro: Deblin is a small garrison town on the Vistula, and in 2011 its oak became the first tree Poland ever voted a national favourite. Grot beat 84 other nominees from across the country in the inaugural Drzewo Roku contest, a huge pedunculate oak at least 500 years old that predates the fortress Tsar Nicholas I later ordered built nearby, a project that cost many of the district's other old trees their lives. Local tradition holds that pressing your left hand to the trunk and whispering a wish will grant it.
meta_description: Deblin's Grot Oak, at least 500 years old and 6 metres round, won Poland's first-ever national tree of the year contest in 2011.
question_meta: Deblin's only remarkable tree is Grot, a pedunculate oak at least 500 years old that won Poland's first Drzewo Roku contest in 2011.
question_answer: Grot, a pedunculate oak standing near ul. Podchorazych in Deblin, is at least 500 years old, 6 metres round and 28 metres tall. It won Poland's first-ever Drzewo Roku (Tree of the Year) contest in 2011, beating 84 other nominated trees from across the country.
question_context: Grot's age comes from local tradition rather than a ring count or a growth-rate calculation: the record simply states it is at least 500 years old, and this site repeats that estimate as given rather than sharpening it into a precise figure. What is documented with more confidence is its size, 6 metres round with a crown spreading 16 metres, and its 2011 win. Klub Gaja, the ecological group that runs Poland's national tree contest, received nominations for 85 trees from 12 voivodeships that year; Grot took the final public vote with nearly 3,500 votes out of more than 15,000 cast, beating Katowice's beech Anton, after students at the town's Gimnazjum nr 2 put its name forward. The oak stands near ul. Podchorazych in the open, with a public geocache marking the spot and dozens of logged visits. Local tradition holds that a wish whispered while pressing your left hand to the bark will come true, a claim this site repeats as tradition rather than fact. The oak may also predate the fortress Tsar Nicholas I ordered built at Deblin, a project that felled many of the district's other old trees.

trees.story:
In 2011, Poland picked its first favourite tree, and an oak outside a small garrison town beat out eighty-four rivals from every corner of the country. Grot, as it is known, took the inaugural Drzewo Roku contest organised by Klub Gaja, edging Katowice's beech Anton in a final round that drew nearly 3,500 votes, out of more than 15,000 cast across the whole contest. Students at the town's Gimnazjum nr 2 had put its name forward.

The tree itself is enormous even before the story starts: a trunk 6 metres round, a crown spreading 16 metres, a height of 28. Nobody has dated it precisely, but the local account puts it at least 500 years old, which would make it older than the fortress Tsar Nicholas I ordered built at Deblin, a project that felled many of the district's other old oaks and left this one standing.

Local tradition has attached a wish to it: press your left hand to the bark and whisper what you want, and it is said to come true. Whether or not that works, the oak has outlasted an empire's garrison and a forest's worth of neighbours to do it, and it stands in the open near ul. Podchorazych with nothing between you and the trunk.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its enormous trunk, 6 metres round, standing alone in the open with a geocache marker nearby. It stands near ul. Podchorazych in Deblin.
